text: All right, well, I'll get going here. I want to start by thanking TPS. Community Learning Connections has been in partnership with TPS for over 26 years now. And we use data and we identify areas of need within our district, and then we leverage community support around those needs. We have focus areas, including the provision of basic needs, student and family supports, mentoring, improving the school climate, and post-secondary success. We have staff in all six buildings working to provide evidence-based programs, and we case manage over 400 students throughout the district. So the provision of basic needs is really like the bread and butter of what we do. We are handing out over 90 Friday food packs a week right now, and we anticipate that going up next semester as more kids get in the building. We also have 100 dairy boxes that we've delivered since the beginning of this school year. And those are donated through Gloria Day, and they have two kinds of meat, milk, cheese, all kinds of things. So those are going to our most at-risk families. And we were able to use some of the grant funding and paid for our guest presenter, Allison Edwards. I think that was back in December, early December. And she spoke to community members about how to help your child with anxiety. There were over 130 parents and teachers that signed up to attend that. And we're really focused on promoting responsible social media use. speaker: kelliglenn
text: Absolutely. Well, back in 2013, the state took a look at its health insurance that's provided to retirees of school systems, and it was underfunded. So the state, in their wisdom, decided they would assign a 3% tax, wage tax on all school employees, which was taxable. The state was then subsequently sued and said, you can't do that. You don't have the authority to do that. And the state came back and said, okay, we don't have the authority to just to sign this, but we'll give employees the option to opt in or opt out of this insurance. If the employee decided to opt in, they were assessed this 3% fee on their wages. And at the time, there was some question whether there should be pre-tax or post-tax, or if it's taxable for the employee. ORS ultimately said this was non-taxable. There was some question. I move that whereas the board of education of Tecumseh schools is locally elected, this locally elected board that is empowered to conduct the business of Tecumseh public schools, pursuing various provisions of the Michigan revised school code. Whereas the district has and continues to navigate how best to meet the educational needs of its students in the midst of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Whereas the district has embraced public act 148 and the requirements of the extended COVID-19 learning plan, which authorizes local elected school boards to determine the learning mode best for its students in cooperation with local health department officials. Whereas the board has reaffirmed on a monthly basis, the learning mode it chooses to extend to students and parents while allowing for parents, staff and public input prior to public vote. Whereas the district administration has developed guidelines to ensure masks are used, social distancing takes place and appropriate public health guides are implemented in each classroom building and school activity. Whereas the board acknowledges the educational benefits of in-person instruction. Whereas the negative effect COVID-19 can have on the societal inequities of those students the district serves, the district programming has sought innovative ways to address concerns for student learning, engagement, mental health and safety. Whereas the board has entered into various contractual agreements with its employee groups to support and enhance protections against the spread of COVID-19. Whereas the district with input from teachers, staff, parents, medical professionals and students has safely operated with 93 days of in-person instruction at the K through eight level for the 2021 school year. Whereas the district consulted with local health officials and followed the board's approved plan, which resulted in either quarantining of staff or students, classrooms or buildings when local metric and data indicated the need. Whereas the district created a plan that has successfully provided parents with an in-person and virtual option for the education of students. Whereas the district administration has and will continue to incorporate appropriate health and safety protocols and standards to successfully restart extracurricular activities, arts and athletic programs, according to Michigan High School Athletic Association, American Choral Directors Association and the National Association of Musical Education and the Educational Theater Association. Whereas the board seeks to have the director of the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services lift any and all restrictions on K through 12 education to allow the board to execute its plan in accordance with public act 148, to provide in-person instruction and programs that are approved by the locally elected board. Whereas one size fits all approach to COVID-19 does not reflect the individual and unique strengths in a district that locally elected board of education can achieve within their community. Now, therefore be it resolved by the locally elected board of education of Tecumseh public schools, we seek to have the authority in the opening and operation of the district's programs and schools in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic in accordance with the requirements of public act 148 and not have its authority rest in an office, board or individual outside of the elected Tecumseh public board of education.

text: On that note, I think that last year's graduation, the drive-in graduation, drive-in theater style graduation we had was, it was done very well. speaker: rickhilderley
text: That's for sure. I like that goal, a large group in-person graduation is a nice goal.

speaker: greg
text: He's being quiet, I think he's done. I don't want to butt in Tony, are you finished? Oh yeah, I'm done. Yeah, sorry. Okay. One of the things Tim said earlier that kind of falls in with our own LSCA or LCSA, whichever that email we got this afternoon. When we talk about, we want control at the lowest level with our district. The one thing that I really think would help would be to have more budgeting type items that are possibly available on the website or they're spelled out better when we have our board meetings. And the reason I feel that way is, I went through the district as an employee for 27 years and I'd always see the first thing that got cut when the budget got tight, which is periodically and Rick went through it too, six, eight years, the budget would go up and then it come down when the first thing we would cut would be athletics. It's 3% of the budget. So you can only cut so much of that as an example. And then when I got selected by, let's see, one, two, three, four of you invited me to come in and be an interim superintendent, that was a real eye-opener. And I had no idea what the cost is of Chromebooks and running Chromebooks. Licensing fees. I didn't have anything to do with that at the time, but licensing fees just so kids can learn online is an expense. Building a tech department is an expense. So when that stuff gets costed out, I agree with what Tim said. There are taxpayers, some of that state money, some of it's local money, regardless of where it comes from. And probably 80 or 90% of our parents don't really care. They just want to see the whole budget balanced and it works. When you look at the expense involved with that, I think that'd be an eye-opener for people to see for those who want to see it. Again, the fact that I hadn't seen it would have been my own fault because I just didn't get that involved, but it's pretty staggering. And it's not just that I just pick it on technology, but when you, I mean, I was just shocked when I looked at the cost that went into Chromebook, Chromebook repair, a technology department, 6 zillion copies being made all the time. We have two ways here to build our budget. Get more students here. That's the ideal way. And then streamline our operations so they're as cost-effective as they can be. And I think when you have people in the community that look at that, good suggestions can come from people in our community who work in businesses or for companies or their CPAs or what have you, where they can take a look at that and say, maybe this is something you could work on. And I think we need to draw on that support from the people we have here that do want to get involved. Because it's, I agree, government at the lowest levels, most effective, because we just saw a big example of how the higher up the food chain you go, it's not necessarily so smooth and effective. So we need to employ that at this level, the end.

speaker: kevinjohnson
text: Thank you, Greg. Yeah, yeah, there's a lot of staggering costs that people don't even consider. I don't know how much we spent last year on toilet paper, but I'm sure it would cause a few heart attacks in town. All those little things add up, that's for sure. You know, and when you look at, people don't really realize that that Chromebook that they can buy for $150 might not be the same Chromebook that they're getting from school. And then the school has to have that licensing for the Chromebook, the software. It all definitely adds up. It seems like the money we saved in textbooks moving to digital was spent two times more in licensing fees sometimes. So transparency in that regard, I think is a good idea. I think with all the documents are available as far as our budget reports and such to the public. However, putting it in a readable format is definitely taxing. Kelly does a pretty good job for us, giving us both the detailed and the CliffsNotes versions. That may be something that we do produce on our website in the future. I think that's worthy of discussion at our next meeting when we're talking about goals for the district to get a little bit more in depth in it.
